title: Three Takeaways from Our Districts Presentation on EdTech and AI
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Parent advocate Emily Cherkin reports on a Seattle Public Schools staff presentation about EdTech and AI use, held after a rally of concerned parents. Her three takeaways are that the district is not listening so much as no longer able to ignore parents, that leaders conflate EdTech with technology education and curriculum with pedagogy, and that heavy child technology use is treated as a foregone conclusion that no one questions. She is sceptical of the announced Gemini ban because it is unclear what was actually blocked, and she notes that GenAI is embedded in tools such as Canva, Book Creator and Word, and that children find workarounds. She cites a new lawsuit alleging harm from a chatbot on a school Chromebook and challenges the superintendent's "abstinence-only" analogy. Her closing demand is that districts prove, access point by access point, that chatbots are really blocked.
points: The district's language of listening to the community masks a shift from ignoring parents to being unable to ignore them.
Leaders blur EdTech (an industry) with technology education (teaching about technology) and treat child technology use as inevitable.
An announced ban on one chatbot means little when GenAI is embedded in existing school apps and students readily find workarounds.
Districts claiming to block GenAI should demonstrate every access point where children could reach it and show that each is closed.
quotes: They aren’t listening to us, but they have realized they cannot ignore us anymore.
They fundamentally do not understand the different between EdTech (an industry like Big Tech) and technology education (teaching ABOUT technology skills— something children desperately need).
No one at the district asked the simple question: “Should children be using so much technology?” or wondered if maybe there were valid reasons to slow down and reevaluate.
This also doesn’t take into account that children find the workarounds— always! Remember— children are curious by nature.
These new “guidelines” also doesn’t take into account the fact that GenAI is embedded within existing EdTech apps that children are already using, like Canva or Book Creator or even Microsoft Word.
If you’re confused that there are so many places where children might even encounter Gemini or AI, you’re not alone and that is entirely the point.
How will Seattle schools— and other districts who claim to “block” GenAI or chatbots— actually prove that they have done so?
